lesson.title: The Conversational Past (Perfekt)
lesson.subtitle: ge- is the old y- (yclept): spoken past with haben/sein + participle at the end

hook.title: The y- You Still Say
hook.content: Chaucer's English stamped its past participles with y-: yclept ('called'), ybounden, ywis ('certainly'). That y- is German ge- — the same ancient prefix, one sound-shift apart. English threw the prefix away almost everywhere... except one word you said this week: enough. Genug is literally ge- + the root of enough — the everyday word where England's ancient participle prefix still lives. Today you build the spoken past with it: haben or sein in position 2, participle closing the bracket — Ich habe es gemacht, Ich bin gekommen.

footnotes.title: yclept, ywis, genug
footnotes.content: Old English ge- weakened to y-/i- in Middle English (yclept = y- + cleopod, 'called'). The prefix then died — but 'enough' (OE ġenōg, ge- + the root) kept its unstressed y- as a plain e-. Genug and enough are the same word, prefix and all.

pattern.title: The Bracket Goes to the Past
pattern.content: Weak verbs (the regulars) build the participle ge- + stem + -t: gemacht, gesagt, gespielt, gelernt. Strong verbs (your ablaut family) build ge- + stem + -en with the vowel changed: gekommen, gegangen, getrunken, gegessen. Choose the auxiliary by meaning: have something DONE → haben (Ich habe gegessen); GO somewhere yourself → sein (Ich bin gekommen, Wir sind gegangen). The -ieren verbs from topic 8 keep their no-ge- privilege: studiert, never gestudiert — and so do ver- verbs: verstanden. Everything lands in the bracket you already own: Ich habe gestern Deutsch gelernt.
pattern.trap_note: Your mind will offer: “every verb builds the past with haben.” Motion and change of state take sein: ich bin gegangen, ich bin gefahren. Ask one question — did I go somewhere, or did I do something to something? Go → sein, do → haben.
pattern.linguist_note: The spoken Perfekt has almost fully replaced the simple past in southern German and colloquial speech — Germans say ich habe gesagt where they once said ich sagte. English did the reverse with 'have said' → 'said'. Two siblings, opposite drifts.

exercises.prompt: Match each participle with its English twin:
exercises.target_answer: gemacht, gesagt, gekommen, gegangen, angekommen, gebucht
exercises.meaning: made, said, come, gone, arrived, booked
exercises.explanation: Weak participles wear ge- + -t; strong ones change the vowel and wear ge- + -en — the same split English shows in made vs come. Separable verbs stack the prefix back on top: an + gekommen.

exercises.prompt: Which form closes the Perfekt bracket: 'Ich habe es _____' (I have made/done it)?
exercises.meaning: Ich habe es gemacht — the ge- participle closes the bracket
exercises.explanation: ge- + stem + -t builds the weak participle: gemacht, gesagt. (It is the same ge- English once wore as y- in yclept.) The calendar loves the bracket too: im Sommer, im Winter, am Wochenende — every calendar word opens a Perfekt story.

exercises.prompt: Build the participle of 'zählen' (tale's twin — count your Minuten by the Minute):
exercises.explanation: ge- + zähl + t = gezählt: the weak participle formula on the counting verb — zählen is the twin of tale, and tell a tale once meant count a tale.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.meaning: I drank a coffee / I have drunk a coffee
cues: The participle is the melody's third note
getrunken sits at the very end
exercises.explanation: The Perfekt bracket: habe in position 2, the strong participle getrunken at the very end. trinken, trank, getrunken — the third note of the melody closes the door.
exercises.affirmation: You caught the participle at the end of the sentence — that is where German always puts it.

exercises.idea: you're telling a friend about last night's study session: you learned German yesterday
idea_parts: the participle → gelernt, ge- + lern + t, at the very end
cues: haben opens, the participle closes: ich habe ... gelernt — ge- + lern + t
exercises.explanation: haben opens the bracket, the participle gelernt closes it — the spoken past is your modal frame wearing ge-.

diagnosis.slip: the helper was chosen by translation, not by motion
diagnosis.cue: haben for things you do (gelernt), sein for movement and change (gekommen). Ask: did the body move?

summary.outcome: Form weak and strong participles and tell yesterday's story in the Perfekt bracket.
summary.takeaway: ge- is the y- of yclept (genug = enough!), haben/sein opens the bracket, the participle closes it.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Strong Verbs & Ancient Ablaut — sing/sang/sung ↔ singen/sang/gesungen: the vowel melody both languages kept.

twist.prompt: Different verb, different helper: I learned German yesterday becomes I CAME yesterday. (Movement picks sein.)
twist.explanation: kommen moves the body, so sein opens the bracket and gekommen closes it — the same y-/ge- prefix, a different helper. You just told yesterday's story twice.

genug.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz with the ancient ge- prefix — the same prefix English wore down to y- (yclept, ywis) and buried inside 'enough'. [wiktionary]

essen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
essen.context_translation: What do we want to eat?
essen.etymology_derivation: Medial t → ss. Noun: das Essen (food).

ankommen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *anakwemana, to come to — an + kommen, with archaic English oncome as the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

buchen.context_translation: I am booking a hotel online.
buchen.etymology_derivation: From Buch plus -en (the beechwood-carving word); the modern reserve sense was modelled after English to book — a semantic loan the page documents. [wiktionary]

hundert.context_phrase: Ein Jahr hat nicht hundert Tage.
hundert.context_translation: A year does not have a hundred days.
hundert.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hundaradą 'hundred-count' — the twin of English hundred. [wiktionary]

minute.etymology_derivation: Medieval Latin minūta — the same Latin loan as English minute. [wiktionary]

zählen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *taljaną, the causative of the tal-root — the same family as English tell and tale; the initial t became z, as in two, zwei. [wiktionary]

wochenende.context_phrase: Am Wochenende fahren wir an den See.
wochenende.context_translation: On the weekend we go to the lake.
wochenende.etymology_derivation: Woche + Ende — the modern compound arose in the 19th century as a calque of English weekend; Woche is the twin of week (k → ch) and Ende the twin of end. [wiktionary]

sommer.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *sumar — English summer is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

winter.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wintruz — English winter is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
